concept: Why do fireflies start flashing in sync?
title: The Meadow That Blinks As One
tagline: A twilight meadow flickers — can a leaderless crowd find a single beat?

science.hiddenLaw: Spontaneous synchronization of pulse-coupled / Kuramoto phase oscillators: each firefly is an oscillator with natural frequency ω_i and phase θ_i that is nudged by neighbors as dθ_i/dt = ω_i + (K/N) Σ_j sin(θ_j - θ_i) (pulse-coupled equivalent: phase advance/delay on seeing a flash), producing a phase-transition to global synchrony with Kuramoto order parameter r→1 when mutual coupling strength K exceeds a critical threshold K_c proportional to the spread of natural frequencies.
science.plainStatement: Each firefly has its own natural blink rate but slightly speeds up or slows down its timer when it sees neighbors flash. When the fireflies pay enough attention to each other, these tiny nudges pull the whole group into the same rhythm and they flash together, with no leader or outside signal needed.
misconceptions: Fireflies synchronize because one leader/pacemaker firefly sets the beat and the rest follow it — predicts removing that one firefly would destroy synchrony.
Synchrony requires fireflies to be identical or to intentionally decide to cooperate — predicts no synchrony is possible with varied natural frequencies or without conscious coordination.

Synchrony is caused by all fireflies responding at once to the same external cue like temperature, darkness, or wind — predicts no synchrony without a shared external pulse and predicts coupling between fireflies is unnecessary.

sources.title: Synchronization of pulse-coupled biological oscillators — Mirollo & Strogatz (1990)
Synchronous rhythmic flashing of fireflies — Buck & Buck, Scientific American (1976)
From Kuramoto to Crawford: exploring the onset of synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators — Strogatz (2000)

story.setting: A misty riverside meadow at dusk in Southeast Asia, where hundreds of fireflies speckle the mangroves with warm pinpricks of light. On some nights the whole bank pulses in sweeping waves of light; on others it stays a restless twinkle.
story.mystery: What makes the meadow switch from chaos to perfect unison? There is no conductor in the trees, and the air is still with no shared flash to cue them. Yet the waves of synchrony come and go as if by invisible agreement.
story.goal: Tune how much the fireflies notice each other, how varied their natural rhythms are, and whether any outside pulse is present. Watch the pattern of flashes and find the hidden rule that lets a leaderless crowd find a beat.

knobs.label: How Much They Notice Neighbors
knobs.hint: Stronger means each flash nudges neighbors more strongly

knobs.label: Diversity of Natural Blink Rates
knobs.hint: Higher means fireflies have more different innate tempos

knobs.label: Bright Conductor Present
knobs.hint: Add a single extra-bright firefly that might act as a leader

knobs.label: Shared Environmental Pulse
knobs.hint: Strength of a common cue like a wind flicker or temperature pulse

knobs.label: Swarm Size
knobs.hint: Number of fireflies in the meadow

predictions.prompt: A dense swarm is flashing in perfect unison. You carefully remove the single brightest firefly that appears to be leading the display. What happens to the group's synchrony a minute later?
options: The swarm falls out of sync — the leader was setting the beat
The swarm stays in sync — the rhythm comes from mutual nudges among all fireflies
The swarm flashes faster and more chaotically without the leader slowing it

predictions.prompt: Two meadows have the same number of fireflies and the same level of mutual attention, but Meadow A has fireflies with almost identical natural blink rates while Meadow B has very diverse natural rates. What does the model predict about their ability to synchronize?
options: Neither can synchronize without a leader deciding to coordinate them
Both will synchronize equally well regardless of diversity
Meadow A will synchronize strongly, Meadow B will stay disordered unless mutual attention is increased to overcome the diversity

predictions.prompt: On a still, uniformly dark night with no wind, temperature pulse, or other shared environmental flash, a large swarm with strong mutual visibility gathers. What does the model predict?
options: No synchrony can appear without a shared external cue to trigger them together
Synchrony can still emerge spontaneously from firefly-to-firefly interactions alone
The fireflies will stop flashing entirely without an external cue

transfer.setup: 80 metronomes with slightly different natural tempos are placed on a light, freely rolling wooden platform that can sway side-to-side. The platform's motion couples the metronomes — a light platform gives strong coupling, a heavy braced table gives weak coupling. There is no conductor metronome and no external ticking sound.
transfer.question: After a few minutes, what will the metronomes do?
options: They will stay out of phase because they have different tempos and no leader to follow
They will spontaneously lock into synchronized ticking through the platform's sway
They will only synchronize if a loud external metronome is added to cue them

checks.description: With strong mutual coupling, similar frequencies, no leader and no external cue, population spontaneously synchronizes to high order parameter
Control: remove the cause — with zero coupling (K=0) synchrony disappears and order parameter stays low
Below critical coupling, even with time to interact, population remains incoherent
With coupling above threshold, order parameter trends upward over time from random initial phases as mutual entrainment builds
With same coupling, larger spread in natural frequencies lowers final synchrony — K_c increases with heterogeneity
